newsitem.title: GERMANY: U.S. army tells 1,100 people technician has HIV.
newsitem.headline: U.S. army tells 1,100 people technician has HIV.

text.p: The U.S. army on Monday said it has begun notifying about 1,100 soldiers and their family members that an army dental hygienist at a German post has tested positive for the HIV virus that causes AIDS.

The hygienist, who provided routine care at the Hanau medical clinic near Frankfurt from February 1995 to June 1996, was removed from direct patient care and sent back to the U.S., the U.S. army medical command in Germany said.
His name and sex were not given,

About 300 soldiers treated by the technician were now serving in Bosnia and neighbouring countries as part of Operation Joint Endeavor and another 300 soldiers and family members have returned to the U.S.
Counselling sessions and tests for the deadly virus were being offered to people who were treated by the person concerned at the Hanau clinic, about 15 miles east of Frankfurt.
An army spokeswoman said about 270 patients have so far come to the Hanau clinic since the announcement was made on Saturday, with 130 being confirmed as having been treated by the technician.
"There has been no hysteria," army spokeswoman Barbara Slifer said. "We have been providing some counselling and those who still have concerns will be tested."

Slifer said the soldier initially tested positive for the HIV virus, which causes Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome, in May and was removed from direct patient care. More testing completed in August showed the solider had the virus.
In 1995, more than 50,000 soldiers in the army's European command were tested for the virus, with 20 being confirmed positive, Slifer said.

U.S. military commanders downplayed the significance of the incident, saying in a statement that "risk assessment officials have determined that the patient risk of contracting the virus from an HIV-infected healthcare provider is zero".
"The scope of the dental hygienist's practice included only basic-level dental hygiene duties, further reducing the likelihood of exposure of the virus to a patient," it said.
The army also said the soldier always wore gloves, mask and gowns and used sterlized instruments during patient care.
The army noted a report by the U.S. Centre for Disease Control that said the only known case of the transfer of the HIV virus from a healthcare provider to a patient was in 1990 in Florida.
A study of more than 22,000 cases showed no case of the virus being transmitted since 1991.
